questions.q: What does a CXPACKET wait actually represent?
options: A parallel worker thread waiting for other threads in the same parallel operation to finish their portion of the work
A thread waiting on a disk I/O operation to complete
A thread waiting for a lock to be released
The server waiting for a client application to send the next request
questions.explain: CXPACKET specifically shows up on parallel query plans, representing coordination waits between parallel worker threads.

questions.q: Why was CXCONSUMER split out from CXPACKET starting in SQL Server 2016?
options: To isolate normal, expected producer/consumer coordination waiting from waits that actually signal a bottleneck, making high CXPACKET a clearer warning sign
Because CXPACKET was renamed and no longer exists
Because parallelism was removed from SQL Server entirely
To track network waits separately from CPU waits
questions.explain: After the split, high CXCONSUMER alone is far less alarming, since it typically reflects expected parallel coordination rather than a genuine problem.

questions.q: What does 'skewed parallelism' mean, per this lesson?
options: One thread in a parallel operation doing most of the actual work while other threads sit nearly idle, often from poor cardinality estimates or uneven data distribution
A query that never goes parallel regardless of its cost
A server with an odd number of NUMA nodes
A query that runs faster serially than in parallel by design
questions.explain: Skew is visible in the execution plan as a wildly uneven row count processed per thread on a parallel operator.

questions.q: If a query shows skewed parallelism, what's the appropriate fix per this lesson, rather than adjusting a parallelism setting?
options: Address the query or statistics side — better cardinality estimates, updated statistics, or a rewrite
Always raise cost threshold for parallelism to a very high value
Always set MAXDOP to 1 for every query on the instance
Rebuild the transaction log
questions.explain: Skew is a query/data problem, not a parallelism-configuration problem — MAXDOP or cost threshold changes won't fix uneven cardinality estimates or skewed data distribution.

questions.q: What does a high total worker time relative to execution count, with no corresponding drop in duration, suggest about a query in sys.dm_exec_query_stats?
options: Parallelism overhead without much payoff — a candidate for a higher cost threshold or a targeted MAXDOP hint
The query is definitely CPU-bound and needs more memory
The query is not using an index and needs one added
The query has a memory leak
questions.explain: Parallel execution trades higher total CPU (worker time) for lower wall-clock duration — if duration doesn't improve, that overhead isn't paying off.
